en: Thus have I heard: the Dīghanakhasutta, the seventy-fourth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain in the Boar’s Cave.
Then the wanderer Dīghanakha approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the wanderer Dīghanakha said this to the Blessed One:
“I, Master Gotama, am of such a doctrine and such a view:
‘Nothing is acceptable to me.
“Even that very view of yours, Aggivessana—”
‘Nothing is acceptable to me’—is even this view of yours not acceptable?
“If, Master Gotama, this view of mine were acceptable, that would be exactly like that; that would be exactly like that.
“In that case, Aggivessana, there are many more people in the world who say: ‘Everything is acceptable to me,’ than those who say: ‘Nothing is acceptable to me.’”
‘That too is exactly like that; that too is exactly like that.
They do not abandon that very view, yet they cling to another view.
Therefore, Aggivessana, those who speak thus are indeed the most meager of the meager in this world.
‘That too is exactly like this; that too is exactly like this.
They abandon that very view and do not adopt another view.
Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins are of such speech and such a view:
‘Everything is acceptable to me,’ Aggivessana;
and some recluses and brahmins, Aggivessana, hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘Nothing is acceptable to me.’
Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘Some things are acceptable to me; some things are not acceptable to me.

But in that regard, Aggivessana, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as ‘Everything is acceptable to me’— [The Blessed One said: “Aggivessana, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this: ‘Some things are acceptable to me; some things are not acceptable to me. Now, Aggivessana, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as ‘Everything is acceptable to me’...”
“This view of theirs, Aggivessana, is close to passion, close to bondage, close to delighting, close to clinging, and close to grasping.
But as for those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘Nothing is acceptable to me’—this view of theirs is close to non-passion, close to non-bondage, close to non-delighting, close to non-clinging, and close to non-grasping.”
When this was said, the wanderer Dīghanakha said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama exalts my own view; Master Gotama thoroughly exalts my own view.
“In that regard, Aggivessana, as for those recluses and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:”
‘Some of it is acceptable to me, some of it is not acceptable to me.
For that view which is acceptable to them stands near to passion, stands near to bondage, stands near to delighting, stands near to clinging, stands near to grasping;
whereas that view which is not acceptable to them stands near to non-passion, stands near to non-bondage, stands near to non-delight, stands near to non-clinging, stands near to non-grasping.
In this regard, Aggivessana, when those ascetics and brahmins hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
"Everything is acceptable to me," a wise person reflects upon that in this way:
‘As for this view of mine:
“Everything is acceptable to me”—
if I were to express this view while stubbornly adhering to it and grasping at it with dogmatic attachment— ’
"This alone is true, all else is false"—
with these two, there would be a dispute for me: namely,
with this ascetic or brahmin who speaks thus and holds such a view as "nothing at all is acceptable to me."
And as for that ascetic or brahmin who speaks thus and holds this view: "Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me"—with these two there is conflict for him.
Thus, when there is conflict, there is dispute; when there is dispute, there is vexation; when there is vexation, there is harassment.
Thus, seeing conflict, dispute, vexation, and distress within himself, he abandons that very view and does not cling to another view.
In this way there is the abandoning of these views; in this way there is the relinquishing of these views.
In this regard, Aggivessana, as for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:
Regarding the thought, "Nothing is acceptable to me," a wise person reflects upon it thus:
"This view of mine— "
If I were to adhere to this view with obstinacy and attachment and declare: "Only this is true, all else is false," thinking, "Nothing is acceptable to me," [that would be a wrong view].
I have two points of contention: first,
that of the ascetic or brahmin who holds this doctrine and view— "Everything is acceptable to me"— and second,
that of the ascetic or brahmin who holds this doctrine and view— "Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me."
With these two, there is conflict for him.
Thus, when there is conflict, there is dispute; when there is dispute, there is vexation; when there is vexation, there is harassment.
Seeing within himself this conflict, dispute, vexation, and harassment, he abandons that very view and does not take up another view.
In this way, there is the abandoning of these views; in this way, there is the relinquishing of these views.
In this regard, Aggivessana, as for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view:
‘Part of it is acceptable to me, part of it is not acceptable to me.’
In this regard, a wise person reflects thus:
"As for this view of mine—
that some things are acceptable to me and some things are not acceptable to me— "
If I were to adhere to this view with obstinacy and attachment and declare:
"This alone is the truth, all else is false," I would have a dispute with two [of these].
Whatever ascetic or brahmin speaks thus and holds this view:
"Everything is acceptable to me," and whatever ascetic or brahmin speaks thus and holds this view:
"Nothing is acceptable to me"—with these two he has a dispute.
"Thus, when there is contention, there is dispute; when there is dispute, there is vexation; when there is vexation, there is harassment.
Seeing within himself this contention, dispute, vexation, and harassment, he abandons that very view and does not take up another view.
In this way, there is the abandoning of these views; in this way, there is the relinquishing of these views.
Furthermore, Aggivessana, this body— possessing form, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and gruel,
subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, and to breaking up and dissolution— should be regarded as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease,
as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.

When one regards this body as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self, whatever desire for the body, affection for the body, or underlying tendency toward the body is abandoned.
Aggivessana, there are these three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
at that time, one experiences only a pleasant feeling.
Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a painful feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
At that time, one experiences only a painful feeling.
Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one experiences neither a pleasant feeling nor a painful feeling;
at that time, one experiences only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Furthermore, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Painful feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation."
Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, disenchanted with painful feeling, and disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises:
"It is liberated. He understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
“Aggivessana, a bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated does not agree with anyone, nor does he dispute with anyone; he employs the common parlance used in the world without clinging to it.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“It seems that for various states, the Blessed One has spoken of abandonment through direct knowledge; it seems that for various states, the Sugata has spoken of relinquishment through direct knowledge.
As the Venerable Sāriputta reflected thus, his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
And in the wanderer Dīghanakha, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose:
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
Then the wanderer Dīghanakha, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma;
having crossed over doubt and being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [even so has this Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama].”
"In this very way, Master Gotama has proclaimed the Dhamma in many ways.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
The Dīghanakhasutta, the fourth, is finished.
